blocks.text: {blue|Probability} measures how likely an event is, on a scale from $0$ (impossible) to $1$ (certain). When outcomes are equally likely, it's a counting exercise:

rows: the same probability in three costumes—convert freely

blocks.text: Strategies

items: **The denominator is the group being drawn from.** Identifying it correctly *is* the skill—most wrong answers are right numerators over wrong denominators.
**Two-way tables:** “and” questions take one cell over the **grand total**.
**“Given that” shrinks the world:** the denominator becomes that row's or column's total, not the grand total.
**Probability predicts counts:** expected number $=$ probability $\times$ group size.

blocks.text: Before computing anything, say the denominator out loud: “out of *all* $200$ students” or “out of *the $120$ eleventh-graders*.” The words of the question always name the group.
A jar holds $5$ red, $7$ blue, and $8$ green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability it is blue?
The Complement: “Not” Questions
For the same jar, what is $P(\text{not green})$? Two roads, one answer:

items.note: Red and blue are the non-greens

blocks.text: Both give $\frac{12}{20} = \frac{3}{5}$. The complement route shines when “not” covers many categories—one subtraction instead of a long addition.

blocks.stem: A box contains $12$ pens: $5$ black, $4$ blue, and $3$ red. If one pen is selected at random, what is the probability that it is **not** blue?

items.text: Not blue means black or red: $\frac{5 + 3}{12} = \frac{8}{12} = \frac{2}{3}$. Or: $1 - \frac{4}{12}$.
$\frac{4}{12} = \frac{1}{3}$ is $P(\text{blue})$—the “not” never got applied.
$\frac{5}{12}$ counts only the black pens, as if “not blue” had one alternative. The red pens are also not blue.
$\frac{7}{12}$ adds blue and red—a complement taken of the wrong color.

blocks.text: Sanity bound: every probability lives in $[0, 1]$, and $P(A) + P(\text{not } A) = 1$. If your two pieces don't sum to $1$, a count is off.
Most SAT probability questions read from a {blue|two-way table}—counts sorted by two categories at once. A survey of $200$ students, by grade and by whether they play a school sport:

blocks.caption: Row and column totals in the margins; the grand total ($200$) in the corner.

blocks.text: If one of the $200$ students is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student plays a sport?

items.note: Column total over the grand total — grade doesn't matter here

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: An **“and”** event names one cell: $P(A \text{ and } B) = \dfrac{\text{that cell}}{\text{grand total}}$ — as long as the draw is from the whole group.

blocks.stem: If one of the $200$ students is selected at random, what is the probability that the student is in grade 11 **and** plays a sport?

items.text: One cell: $72$ grade-11 athletes, out of all $200$ students: $\frac{72}{200} = \frac{9}{25}$.
$\frac{72}{120} = \frac{3}{5}$ divides by the grade-11 total—that answers a **given that** question (“given grade 11…”), which this is not.
$\frac{72}{90} = \frac{4}{5}$ divides by the athletes' total—the other conditional, also not asked.
Multiplying the two overall probabilities assumes grade and sport are unrelated—the table shows they aren't (grade 11 plays at a much higher rate). Read the cell; don't reconstruct it.

blocks.text: Check a table's health before using it: rows sum to their margins, margins sum to the grand total. Ten seconds, and it also forces you to *see* where everything lives.

blocks.label: Rule
blocks.text: **Conditional probability:** “given that $B$” restricts the draw to group $B$. The denominator becomes $B$'s total; the numerator is the part of $B$ that is also $A$.
Same table as before. *Given that a student is in grade 11*, what is the probability the student plays a sport? The words “given grade 11” collapse the world to that one row of $120$ students:

items.note: Athletes within the row, over the **row total**

blocks.text: Compare: overall, $P(\text{sport}) = \frac{90}{200} = 45\%$—but *within grade 11* it's $60\%$. Conditioning changed the answer because the two grades behave differently. And the **direction** of conditioning matters too:
Same cell on top ($72$), different worlds below—$\frac{3}{5}$ versus $\frac{4}{5}$. The condition always names the denominator.

blocks.stem: One student is selected at random from those who do **not** play a sport. What is the probability that the student is in grade 12?

items.text: “From those who do not play” makes the world the $110$ non-athletes; $62$ of them are twelfth-graders: $\frac{62}{110} = \frac{31}{55}$.
$\frac{62}{200} = \frac{31}{100}$ uses the grand total—but the draw was never from all $200$ students.
$\frac{62}{80} = \frac{31}{40}$ conditions in the wrong direction: that's $P(\text{no sport} \mid \text{grade 12})$.
$\frac{110}{200} = \frac{11}{20}$ is just the probability of being a non-athlete—the *condition*, not the question.

blocks.text: Watch for conditioning in disguise: “of the students who…,” “among those that…,” “selected from…”—all mean **given that**, and all shrink the denominator.
Probability from a Frequency Table
One-variable frequency data works the same way—the denominator is the total frequency. Twenty students reported the number of books they read last month:

blocks.stem: If one of the $20$ students is chosen at random, what is the probability that the student read **at least** $2$ books?

items.text: $\frac{5}{20} = \frac{1}{4}$ counts only *exactly* $2$—“at least” includes everything above it.
$\frac{13}{20}$ is the complement—the students who read **fewer than** $2$.
$\frac{7}{13}$ divides favorable by *unfavorable*. Probabilities compare with the **total**, never part-to-part.

blocks.text: From Probability to Predicted Counts
Probability runs forward, too: applied to a group, it **predicts a count**.
Quality testing shows that the probability a randomly selected part is defective is $0.02$. About how many defective parts should be expected in a shipment of $1{,}500$?

items.note: Probability $\times$ group size — about $30$ defective parts

blocks.text: Words like “expected,” “predicted,” or “about how many” signal this move—and the answer is an estimate, so it needn't divide evenly in real life.
For every question, name the denominator's group **before** computing—then check whether a “given that” (in any disguise) shrinks it.

blocks.stem: A bag contains $6$ apple, $9$ grape, and $5$ cherry candies. If one candy is drawn at random, what is the probability that it is **not** grape?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Total $= 6 + 9 + 5 = 20$; not-grape $= 6 + 5 = 11$, so $P = \frac{11}{20}$ (equivalently $1 - \frac{9}{20}$).

items.text: $\frac{9}{20}$ is $P(\text{grape})$—the complement was never taken.
$\frac{6}{20} = \frac{3}{10}$ counts only apple, forgetting cherry is also not grape.
$\frac{11}{9}$ is greater than $1$—impossible for a probability, and a part-to-part ratio besides.

blocks.stem: The table classifies $150$ workers by commute type and shift. If one worker is selected at random, what is the probability that the worker takes public transit **and** works the evening shift?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** “And” names one cell—$36$ transit-evening workers—over the grand total: $\frac{36}{150} = \frac{6}{25}$.

items.text: One cell over $150$. {green|✓}
$\frac{36}{60} = \frac{3}{5}$ divides by the transit row—that's $P(\text{evening} \mid \text{transit})$, a conditional that wasn't asked.
$\frac{36}{72} = \frac{1}{2}$ divides by the evening column—the other unasked conditional.
$\frac{60}{150} = \frac{2}{5}$ is just $P(\text{transit})$—the “and” half is missing.

blocks.stem: Using the same table: if the selected worker is known to work the **morning shift**, what is the probability that the worker drives?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** “Known to work the morning shift” shrinks the world to that column's $78$ workers, of whom $54$ drive: $\frac{54}{78} = \frac{9}{13}$.

items.text: Cell over **column total**—the condition names the denominator. {green|✓}
$\frac{54}{150} = \frac{9}{25}$ uses the grand total, ignoring the condition entirely.
$\frac{54}{90} = \frac{3}{5}$ conditions the wrong way: that's $P(\text{morning} \mid \text{drives})$.
$\frac{78}{150} = \frac{13}{25}$ is the probability of the *condition* (morning shift), not of driving within it.

blocks.stem: The probability that a certain team wins any given game is $\frac{3}{8}$. If the team plays $240$ games, about how many games should the team be expected to win?

answer.text: **The correct answer is A.** Expected count $=$ probability $\times$ group size: $\frac{3}{8} \times 240 = 90$.

items.text: $240 \div 8 = 30$ per eighth, times $3$. {green|✓}
$80$ is $\frac{1}{3}$ of $240$—the fraction $\frac{3}{8}$ flipped into “one in three.”
$150$ is $\frac{5}{8} \times 240$—the expected **losses**, the complement.
$30$ is $240 \div 8$: one eighth, with the $3$ never applied.

blocks.title: Things to Remember
items: $P = \frac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}}$, always between $0$ and $1$. Fractions, decimals, and percents are interchangeable.
**The denominator is the group being drawn from**—say it before you compute.
Two-way tables: “$A$ and $B$” $=$ one cell over the **grand total**. Check that rows and columns sum to their margins.
“Given that,” “of those who,” “selected from” → conditional: the denominator becomes that **row or column total**. Direction matters: $P(A \mid B) \neq P(B \mid A)$.
$P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$; the two must sum to $1$. “At least $k$” includes $k$ and everything above.
